title: Chalmers warns of slower growth as traders bet on rate rise next month
full_text:
Treasurer Jim Chalmers will warn of slower economic growth and higher unemployment as officials rework numbers ahead of the Albanese government’s mid-year update, and traders price in a two-in-three chance the Reserve Bank of Australia will lift rates for a fifth time this year.
Chalmers’ comments will come after the RBA wrote to a parliamentary committee, acknowledging that lower government spending would ultimately reduce inflation, helping hold off interest rate rises.
“While the composition of a specific spending proposal matters, in general lower government spending would reduce aggregate demand unless it was offset by stronger spending elsewhere,” the letter, sent after an appearance by RBA governor Michele Bullock last month, reads. “If this eased capacity pressures, it would also tend to reduce inflationary pressures.”
The letter, and Chalmers’ speech at Citi A50 Economic Forum on Friday, come amid debate between economists and the government about what is driving the persistently high inflation that has pushed the RBA to increase rates to 4.6 per cent. That is its highest level in 15 years.
The government has downplayed its own role in driving up inflation, blaming a long conflict in the Middle East for driving up the price of materials, particularly fuel, along with heavy spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure that has also fuelled price and wage rises.
“We’re not immune from the consequences of two wars, both impacting almost every economy in one way or another, posing risks to global growth, pushing up global inflation, and pushing up borrowing costs,” Chalmers will tell the forum in Sydney ahead of the crucial economic update in December.
“Treasury is in the process of revising all the numbers for the mid-year update. Higher interest rates and higher inflation are likely to mean softer growth and slightly higher unemployment,” he will say, according to a copy of his prepared remarks circulated on Thursday afternoon.
Still, the update is expected to flag an additional $50 billion in business investment, which is largely related to demand for data centre construction.
Real government spending grew at 4.3 per cent in the past financial year, more than double the 1.8 per cent growth rate projected in the 2024 budget. That has put spending at a 40-year high outside the pandemic.
Headline inflation jumped to 4 per cent in August, and many economists are predicting little to change when quarterly figures are published next week.
On Wednesday, RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser warned the outlook was “materially worse” since the central bank updated its public forecasts in August, prompting traders to price in a 64 per cent chance of a rate rise next month. That was up from 27 per cent before Hauser’s speech.
The RBA’s letter to a parliamentary committee followed a long exchange between Bullock, RBA chief economist Sarah Hunter, and Simon Kennedy, the Coalition’s assistant finance spokesman, at a hearing last month.
Bullock and Hunter avoided being directly drawn on the impact on the economy of a hypothetical cut to public spending, telling Kennedy that the RBA had not recently modelled such a scenario. However, that appeared to contradict modelling released by the RBA in April in response to freedom of information requests which examined two such scenarios.
In both cases, reduced public spending triggered a decline in inflation that dropped below 2.5 per cent, the mid-point of the RBA’s target range.
The RBA noted the modelling in its letter, adding changes in government spending on inflation were not “mechanical or one-for-one” while acknowledging generally the potential for a reduction to curb inflation.
“Estimating the effect of a specific policy proposal would require further detail about what spending would be reduced, when the reduction would occur and how other parts of the economy might respond,” it said.
Kennedy said the government should cut spending. “The RBA has confirmed in writing that reining in government spending can help ease inflationary pressures. Australians cannot be left to do all the heavy lifting,” he said.
Warren Hogan, the chief economic advisor at specialist business lender Judo Bank, said while the RBA’s approach to Kennedy’s questions rightfully avoided giving elected officials advice on fiscal policy, the central bank’s officials had cut the government “a bit too much slack”.
“They don’t want to embarrass the government, but they’re going to have to do things which are politically uncomfortable,” said Hogan of the prospect that the RBA would have to continue raising interest rates.
That lower government spending can reduce inflation has been acknowledged by several commentators, including former RBA officials.
In a podcast published by the Institute of Public Affairs last month, former RBA governor Philip Lowe said the government should be running budget surpluses to curb inflation and take the pressure off interest rates.
“We find ourselves running sizeable budget deficits at a time when we’re at full employment and commodity prices are very high. We should be running sizeable surpluses,” Lowe told IPA chief economist Adam Creighton.
